title: Spelling from Dictation
keyIdea: To write a sentence someone says to you, first say it back and count the words so you can hold it in your head. Then write one word at a time, saying each word slowly and putting one grapheme for each sound: ship is sh-i-p, three sounds. Some sounds need two or three letters (sh, ai, ck, igh, oa). Tricky words such as said, was and they do not follow the sound rules, so you learn them by heart. Last, read it back and check for a capital letter, a full stop and the tricky words.
familyTip: Say a short sentence about your day, like We had fish for tea. Your child says it back and holds up a finger for each word, then writes it. Do not show it. Read their writing together: did every word make it, is there a capital and a full stop, and are said or was spelt the tricky way?

visual.caption: Can you spell it by its sounds, or is it a tricky word? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: count the words, spell each sound, pick the tricky words, write a sentence from memory and check it.

kid: A grown-up says a sentence. You write it. First say it back. Count the words on your fingers. Now you can hold it in your head.
Write one word at a time. Say the word slowly. Each sound gets its letters. ship has three sounds: sh, i, p. sh is two letters but one sound.
Some words are tricky. said does not look like it sounds. You learn tricky words by heart. Look, cover, write, check.
Then read it back. Is there a capital at the start? Is there a full stop at the end? Did you spell said and was the tricky way?
adult: Ages 5 to 8. The National Curriculum in England asks Year 1 pupils to write from memory simple sentences dictated by the teacher that include words using the grapheme-phoneme correspondences (GPCs) and common exception words taught so far, and Year 2 pupils to do the same with longer sentences and punctuation. Lower Key Stage 2 extends this to words and punctuation taught so far. In the US, Common Core L.1.2d and L.1.2e ask for conventional spelling of common patterns and frequent irregular words and phonetic spelling of untaught words, and L.2.2d asks children to generalise learned spelling patterns.

Dictation joins three skills. Holding the sentence is working memory: saying it back and counting words stops children dropping small words such as a, is and at. Segmenting is breaking a word into phonemes and choosing a grapheme for each one: a digraph (sh, ai, ck, oa) is two letters for one sound and a trigraph (igh) is three. Common exception words (said, was, they, the, have, come, one) have parts that do not match the taught GPCs, so they are practised as whole spellings.

Common mistakes: counting letters instead of sounds (s-h-i-p as four), writing ay in the middle of a word (rayn) or ck after a long vowel, spelling exception words by sound (sed, woz, thay), losing a small word from the sentence, and leaving out the capital or full stop because attention went on the spelling. A phonically plausible error like sed shows the child is segmenting well; the next step is to learn that word as an exception.

In the lab your child counts the words in four sentences, picks the grapheme for each sound in five words (ship, rain, duck, night, boat), chooses the right spelling of seven common exception words, hides a sentence and rebuilds it from memory three times, and finds the capital, full stop and tricky-word slips in four written sentences.

practice.prompt: How many sounds are in ship?
practice.hint: Say it slowly. Is sh one sound or two?
practice.explain: sh is one sound made by two letters, so ship is sh-i-p: three sounds and four letters.

practice.prompt: A sentence has {a} words. Your child wrote {b} of them. How many words are missing?
practice.hint: Take the words written away from all the words in the sentence.
practice.explain: {a} words take away {b} written leaves {=a-b} missing. Counting words before writing helps stop this.

practice.hint: said is a tricky word. It does not match its sounds.
practice.explain: said sounds like sed but is spelt s-a-i-d. It is a common exception word to learn by heart.

practice.prompt: A word has {n} sounds. Each sound gets one box. How many boxes do you draw?
practice.hint: One box for each sound, not for each letter.
practice.explain: {n} sounds need {=n} boxes. A digraph like sh still fits in one box.

practice.prompt: How do you spell the /ai/ sound in the middle of rain?
practice.hint: ay usually goes at the end of a word.
practice.explain: In the middle of a word the /ai/ sound is usually ai (rain, tail). ay is used at the end (play, day).

pool.prompt: Which word is a tricky word?
pool.hint: Which one does not match its sounds?
pool.explain: was sounds like woz but is spelt w-a-s. cat and ship match their sounds.

pool.prompt: How do you spell the end sound in duck?
pool.hint: The sound comes straight after a short vowel.
pool.explain: Right after a short vowel like u, the k sound is spelt ck: duck, sock, back.

pool.prompt: How many words are in: The dog is on the mat.
pool.hint: Count each word on a finger, even the small ones.
pool.explain: The, dog, is, on, the, mat: six words. Small words like is are easy to miss.

pool.hint: Check the start and the end.
pool.explain: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop: We had fun.

pool.prompt: How do you spell the long i sound in night?
pool.hint: It is a trigraph: three letters for one sound.
pool.explain: In night, light and high the long i sound is spelt igh, three letters for one sound.

pool.prompt: A sentence has {a} words and {b} of them are tricky words. How many are not tricky words?
pool.hint: Take the tricky words away from all the words.
pool.explain: {a} words take away {b} tricky ones leaves {=a-b} that follow the sound rules.

pool.prompt: A word has {n} sounds. One of them is a digraph, two letters for one sound. How many letters does it have?
pool.hint: Every sound has one letter, but the digraph has one extra.
pool.explain: {n} sounds with one digraph gives {n} + 1 = {=n+1} letters. ship has 3 sounds and 4 letters.

pool.prompt: What do you do first when someone says a sentence for you to write?
choices: Say it back and count the words
pool.hint: How do you hold a sentence in your head?
pool.explain: Saying it back and counting the words holds the whole sentence in your head before you start.

pool.prompt: Which is the right spelling of they?
pool.hint: they is a tricky word. It ends in ey.
pool.explain: they is a common exception word: t-h-e-y. thay is a good try by sound, but not the spelling.
